newsitem.title: CHINA: China says share offers abroad need approval.
newsitem.headline: China says share offers abroad need approval.

text.p: China said on Friday that Chinese-controlled companies making share offers abroad must obtain approval from domestic regulators.

State television, quoting a directive from the State Council or cabinet, also said the government must approve all transfers of domestic assets into Chinese-controlled companies abroad if the purpose of the transaction is to inject the assets into a listed vehicle.
Television said regulators wanted all foreign offers of stock by Chinese companies to be made as direct listings.
It did not specifically rule out indirect listings such as the now popular red chips in Hong Kong but it suggested this would be frowned upon in future.
Red chips are Chinese-controlled companies incorporated in Hong Kong. They have been hugely popular with investors, partly due to expectations of injections of assets from mainland China.

The television statement said Chinese entities or major shareholders must first obtain approval from provincial level authorities or the State Council before transferring assets to a foreign based company owned by Chinese interests for the purpose of making a stock listing.
The China Securities Regulatory Commission, the key stock market regulator, would review the proposal and the Securities Commission of the State Council would decide on approval.
Final approval would be based on the annual quota for share offers and that any form of asset transfer was covered by the regulation.
State television also warned that companies issuing shares outside the country without regulatory approval would be punished. It did not give any details.

The directive, which said the regulations were aimed at improving regulation of the market, also repeated a previous ban on the purchase of shell companies for the purpose of obtaining a foreign listing.
Shell company purchases once were a popular form of gaining a quick foreign listing, usually in Hong Kong, but they have largely been overshadowed by new listings of red chips in recent years.

The regulations also said that Chinese controlled companies abroad that had invested in mainland China would not be allowed to list the domestic assets on an overseas market until three years after the investment was made.
